title: 진짜 vs 정말 vs 참
rule: 진짜 and 정말 are near-interchangeable — 진짜 is what you say with friends and in texts, 정말 is safe everywhere including writing. 참 is different in feel: a soft, warm 'really' that mostly shows up in gentle compliments and observations.

members.hint: safe in speech and writing alike

example.en: The weather is really nice today.

title: 너무 vs 아주 vs 되게
rule: 너무 is the everyday spoken intensifier and works for good things and bad things alike — 너무 좋아요 is completely normal, so don't treat it as 'negative only'. 아주 is the plain, neutral 'very' that also fits formal writing, and 되게 is 너무's casual twin: fine in speech and texts with friends, but out of place in anything formal.

members.hint: the go-to spoken intensifier, either way

example.en: I love this song so much.
The coffee here is very good.

members.hint: casual talk only, not formal writing

title: 미안해요 vs 죄송해요 vs 죄송합니다
rule: Pick by who you are apologizing to: 미안해요 for friends, peers and people younger than you; 죄송해요/죄송합니다 for strangers, seniors, customers and your boss. Between those two, 죄송해요 is softer and everyday, 죄송합니다 is the formal one you use at work or when the mistake is serious.

members.hint: for people close to you or below you
the gentler polite apology to strangers

example.en: I'm sorry to keep you waiting.
I'm truly sorry for being late.

title: 알겠어요 vs 알았어요
rule: Both mean 'okay, got it', but 알겠어요 is the safe one for accepting instructions from anyone. 알았어요 is the same okay with a shrug — with the wrong tone it lands as 'yeah, yeah, I know', so save it for people you're close to.

title: 괜찮아요 vs 좋아요 vs 됐어요
rule: When someone offers you something, 좋아요 accepts it and 괜찮아요 turns it down politely ('I'm fine, thanks'). 됐어요 also refuses, but bluntly — close to 'forget it' — so beginners should stay with 괜찮아요.

members.hint: a clear yes to an offer

example.en: Yes, sounds good! Let's go together.

members.hint: a curt 'no thanks' that sounds annoyed

example.en: Never mind, I'll do it myself.

title: 감사합니다 vs 고맙습니다 vs 고마워요
rule: 감사합니다 and 고맙습니다 are equally polite and swappable — 감사합니다 is what you hear most in shops and at work, 고맙습니다 sounds a little warmer and more personal. 고마워요 is the softer 요-form for people you already know, not for a boss or a customer.

members.hint: just as polite, a touch warmer
the softer 요-form for people you know

title: 같이 vs 함께
rule: They mean the same thing and are almost always swappable; 같이 is what people actually say out loud every day, while 함께 sounds a bit warmer and more polished, so it turns up in writing, invitations and slogans.

members.hint: the one you actually say out loud
same meaning, a bit more polished

example.en: It's even better if we go together.

title: 빨리 vs 일찍 vs 어서
rule: 빨리 is about speed and 일찍 is about the clock: 빨리 오세요 means 'get here quick', 일찍 오세요 means 'come at an early hour'. 어서 also pushes for speed but sounds warm and welcoming, so it lives in polite invitations like 어서 오세요.

members.hint: about speed, and can sound impatient
about the clock, not the speed
warm urging, mostly with polite invitations

title: 잘 vs 자주
rule: These are not two shades of one word: 잘 answers "how well?" (skill, quality) and 자주 answers "how often?" (number of times), so swapping them changes the meaning entirely, not the nuance. One overlap to know: with things that happen to you, 잘 can mean "easily, tends to" (감기에 잘 걸려요 = "I catch colds easily") — but for a plain count of times, it is always 자주.

members.hint: about how well, not how many times
about how often, never how well

title: 그리고 vs 그래서 vs 그런데 vs 그러면
rule: Pick by the logical link back to the sentence you just said: 그리고 simply adds, 그래서 gives its result, 그런데 turns away from it, and 그러면 treats it as a premise ("if that's so, then…"). Note that in real speech 그런데/근데 is very often not contrast at all — it's just "by the way", a way to slide into a new topic.

example.en: I had dinner. And then I drank coffee.
It's raining. So I'm staying home.

members.when: soft contrast, or changing the topic

example.en: By the way, when are we meeting?

members.when: reacting to what was just said

title: 아마 vs 혹시 vs 어쩌면
rule: 아마 and 어쩌면 are guesses that differ in confidence: 아마 leans yes ("probably"), 어쩌면 just opens a real possibility ("maybe, who knows"). 혹시 is not a guess at all — it fronts a question or request to soften it, like "by any chance".

members.hint: your best guess — pairs with -ㄹ 거예요

example.en: Do you have time, by any chance?

members.hint: less sure than 아마 — "maybe, who knows"

example.en: Maybe I won't be able to go.

title: 조금 vs 좀 vs 약간
rule: For real amounts all three overlap — 좀 is simply the spoken contraction of 조금, and 약간 is the cooler, more written "slightly". The deciding fact is that only 좀 has a second life as a request softener, where it means "please / if you would" and not "a little" at all (물 좀 주세요).

members.hint: the full form — speech and writing alike

example.en: Could I get some water, please?

title: 다 vs 모두 vs 전부
rule: 다 is the short spoken default and almost always sits right before the verb (밥 다 먹었어요). 모두 and 전부 are nouns as well, so they take particles freely (모두가 왔어요, 전부를 샀어요) — 다 mostly doesn't, apart from set phrases like 이게 다예요 ("that's all"). Between 모두 and 전부, 모두 leans toward people ("everyone"), 전부 toward things and totals ("the whole lot"), though in most sentences they swap freely.

members.when: everyday speech, right before the verb
members.hint: the short spoken default — almost always adverbial
can be a noun; leans toward people

members.when: the whole amount, nothing left out
members.hint: "the whole lot" — leans toward things, totals

example.en: How much is all of this?

title: 이제 vs 지금 vs 방금 vs 아까
rule: 지금 just points at this exact moment, while 이제 says the situation has changed ("now, unlike before"). The two past ones split purely by depth: 방금 is seconds to a couple of minutes ago, 아까 is earlier today.

example.en: What are you doing right now?

members.hint: "a second ago" — the tightest recent past

title: 먼저 vs 우선 vs 일단
rule: 먼저 is plain order — this action or person comes before that one. 우선 and 일단 both mean "first, before anything else" and often swap in speech; they differ in what they lean on: 우선 points at what matters most ("first and foremost"), 일단 at what's provisional ("let's do this much for now and sort out the rest later").

members.hint: plain "before the other thing or person"

members.when: what matters most, do it first
members.hint: "first and foremost" — or just "to begin with"

title: 재미있다 vs 즐겁다 vs 웃기다
rule: 재미있다 is the default for anything entertaining or interesting — a movie, a game, a class. 즐겁다 is the pleasant feeling of an activity or time spent together (and the fixed word in wishes like 즐거운 하루 보내세요), while 웃기다 specifically means it makes you laugh.

members.hint: the pleasant feeling of doing something

title: 예쁘다 vs 아름답다 vs 귀엽다
rule: 예쁘다 is the everyday default for anything nice to look at, and it is what you'll say 90% of the time. Reach for 아름답다 only when you're genuinely moved (scenery, music, a moment), and 귀엽다 when the appeal is small-and-lovable rather than good-looking.

members.hint: about lovable charm, not good looks

title: 말하다 vs 이야기하다
rule: Use 말하다 for producing words — saying one thing, or speaking a language. Use 이야기하다 when there's a back-and-forth or a story being told: chatting with someone, usually marked with 와/과 or 하고.

members.hint: the two-way chat verb, with 하고/와

title: 만나다 vs 보다
rule: 만나다 is the neutral "meet" and is never wrong. But in real casual speech Koreans constantly use 보다 with a person — 내일 봐요, 친구 봤어요 — so 보다 means "see / hang out with" someone you already know, while 만나다 fits arranged or first-time meetings.

members.when: casual meet-ups with people you know

title: 알다 vs 알아보다 vs 알아듣다
rule: 알다 is having the information already; 알아보다 is going out to find it (or making out a face you half-recognize); 알아듣다 is catching the words someone just said to you. If your problem is your ears, it's 알아듣다.

members.when: checking something out, recognizing a face
members.hint: going to find out, or recognizing by sight

title: 기다리다 vs 기대하다
rule: These are false friends for English "wait for / expect." 기다리다 is actual waiting — time passing until someone or something arrives. 기대하다 is looking forward to something good, with no waiting around involved.

members.when: waiting for a person, bus, turn

example.en: I'm looking forward to the trip.

title: 끝나다 vs 마치다
rule: Ask who does the ending. If the thing ends on its own, use 끝나다 with 이/가 (수업이 끝났어요). If a person brings it to a close, the everyday word is 끝내다 with 을/를 (일을 끝냈어요). 마치다 is the more formal, "properly concluded" version of that — 오늘 일을 마쳤어요 — and you'll also hear it on its own (수업 마치고 갈게요), so treat it as the polished option rather than the default.

members.hint: it ends by itself — takes 이/가

members.when: you bring something to a close
members.hint: the formal "finish it" — everyday word is 끝내다

title: 시작하다 vs 출발하다
rule: English "start" covers both, but Korean never mixes them: 시작하다 is an activity beginning (class, work, a movie), 출발하다 is a person or vehicle physically leaving the starting point. You can 출발하다 for school and 시작하다 the class after you arrive.

members.hint: physically setting off from a place

title: 그렇군요 vs 아 그래요? vs 그러니까요
rule: Pick by what you're reacting to: 그렇군요 for a new fact you're quietly taking in, 아 그래요? for news that mildly surprises you and invites them to say more, 그러니까요 for agreeing hard with an opinion or complaint you already felt yourself.

example.en: Ah, I see. I didn't know that.
Oh really? When did you go?

members.when: agreeing with a complaint or opinion

title: 안녕히 가세요 vs 안녕히 계세요
rule: Ask one question: who is walking away? Say 안녕히 가세요 to the person who leaves, and 안녕히 계세요 if you are the one leaving — so 안녕히 계세요 is what you say on your way out of a shop or someone's home.

members.hint: what you say to the person leaving
your goodbye as you walk out

title: 별로 vs 전혀 vs 거의
rule: All three normally need a negative predicate (별로 안 좋아요, 전혀 몰라요, 거의 안 가요): use 별로 for a soft "not really", 전혀 for a flat zero, and 거의 for "hardly ever". Only 거의 also works with a positive verb, where it means "almost" (거의 다 왔어요).

members.hint: the absolute zero — needs a negative

example.en: I don't know that person at all.
I hardly watch TV these days.

title: 곧 vs 이따가 vs 나중에
rule: How far away is it? 곧 is minutes from now, 이따가 is later but still today, and 나중에 is an open, unpromised future — which is why 나중에 is the polite way to put something off.

members.hint: later today, hours away at most

example.en: I'll call you again later today.

members.hint: a vague later — maybe another day

title: 항상 vs 늘 vs 보통
rule: 항상 and 늘 both mean "always" and swap freely — 늘 is a little more literary and shows up most in set wishes like 늘 건강하세요, so 항상 is the safe default in speech. 보통 is the real contrast: it means "usually" and leaves room for exceptions.

members.hint: the same "always", more literary — common in wishes

example.en: I usually get up at seven.

title: 벌써 vs 이미 vs 아직
rule: 벌써 and 이미 differ in tone, not timing: 벌써 reacts with surprise ("already?!"), while 이미 just reports a settled fact. 아직 is the opposite pole — "not yet" with a negative verb, "still" with a positive one.

title: 하지만 vs 그렇지만 vs 그래도
rule: 하지만 and 그렇지만 are both a plain "but" and swap freely — 하지만 is the one you'll hear more in speech, 그렇지만 sounds a touch more careful. Reach for 그래도 only when you mean "even so": you accept the fact and do it anyway.

example.en: Kimchi is spicy. But it's delicious.
Korean is difficult. But it's fun.
It's expensive. Even so, I'm going to buy it.

title: 힘들다 vs 어렵다 vs 피곤하다
rule: English "hard" splits in two here: 힘들다 is tough and draining (on your body or your heart), while 어렵다 is difficult to do or understand. 피곤하다 isn't "hard" at all — it describes you being tired, not the task.

members.hint: difficult — a puzzle, not a burden
tired — the person, not the task

example.en: I'm tired because I couldn't sleep.

title: 묻다 vs 물어보다 vs 질문하다
rule: 물어보다 is what people actually say out loud; 묻다 is the same act but terser and more written (and ㄷ-irregular, so it becomes 물어요). 질문하다 is "ask a question" where questions are a formal event — a class, a meeting, a Q&A.

example.en: I asked for directions at the station.

members.hint: the normal spoken "ask" — use this one
asking a question in a formal setting

example.en: I asked a question during class.
